papers.authors: Markus Krimmel, Louis Milliken, Ekaterina Glazkova, Maximilian Schall, Antoine Chaffin, Sedigheh Eslami, Jonas Golde, Denis Bykov, Claire Beamer, Jeremy Yang, Bo Wang
papers.summary: Perplexity releases 0.6B and 9B multi-vector retrievers that encode text, images, and document screenshots: each document token stores a 128-d vector, and scoring sums MaxSim of each query vector against document vectors. Both models distill token-by-token from the same 18B teacher, ==so they share one vector space== and a 9B offline document index can be queried by a 0.6B online encoder. On 72 domain retrieval tasks the 9B model averages nDCG@10 81.3%, 1.6 points above nemotron-3-embed-8b; a 0.6B query with a 9B index scores 79.6%, above 78.0% when both ends use 0.6B. deep_reading.title: pplx-embed-v2-late Technical Report
deep_reading.content:
Perplexity releases two multi-vector retrieval models, pplx-embed-v2-late at 0.6B and 9B, that encode text, images, and document page screenshots. They are late-interaction retrievers: every document token stores a 128-d vector, every query token gets a vector, and scoring sums MaxSim—each query vector takes its max inner product against document vectors. The two models are not trained separately with contrastive learning; they ==both distill token-by-token from the same 18B teacher's output vectors==, so they live in one vector space: the corpus can be indexed offline with 9B and queried online with 0.6B. On the authors' 72 domain retrieval tasks, 9B averages nDCG@10 81.3%, 1.6 points above next-best nemotron-3-embed-8b; a 0.6B query with a 9B index scores 79.6%, 1.6 points above both ends at 0.6B, with unchanged query-side cost. Note that the full list of the 72 tasks is not public, so the scores cannot be independently reproduced.

## 1. Why late interaction, why distill

Retrievers usually trade off between single-vector ANN (fast, loses detail) and cross-encoders (strong, one pass per candidate, only for reranking). Late interaction sits in between: document token vectors are precomputed; at query time only query vectors are computed, then MaxSim. Storage is the cost, so this work compresses each token vector to 128-d.

The authors' other judgment: small models trained with contrastive learning alone are not strong enough; fitting a large model's token vectors works better. A side effect is that differently sized students distilled from the same teacher are interchangeable.

## 2. Training

### 2.1 18B teacher: two-stage contrastive learning

The teacher is Qwen3.5-27B with the last 20 layers dropped (18B) and causal masks removed so every token sees both sides. Training has two stages.

Stage 1 uses query–document pairs from 28 datasets, further split by language and domain into 981 subsets, 186M pairs total (88.3% text–text, 8.3% text–image, 3.4% text–screenshot); sampling weights change the mix to 56.5% / 30.9% / 12.6%. Each batch comes from one subset so in-batch negatives are harder. To hit target mix and even spacing, subsets are sampled with a golden-ratio quasi-random sequence rather than independent draws. Contrastive batch size is 16,384 pairs, LoRA rank 128; MaxSim is a Triton kernel to avoid materializing the token-level similarity matrix.

Stage 2 merges LoRA, adds a new rank-32 adapter, freezes vision, and trains only on text triples: each query with one positive and up to 4 hard negatives. Some hard negatives are synthesized by editing key fields in highly templated documents.

### 2.2 Students: token-wise fit to teacher vectors

Student loss is direct: for every valid query and document token, Euclidean distance between L2-normalized student and teacher vectors, averaged on the query side and document side then summed. The teacher is frozen.

$$\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{Q}}\lVert q^S_{it}-q^T_{it}\rVert_2+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{D}}\lVert d^S_{it}-d^T_{it}\rVert_2$$

Because the loss needs no in-batch negatives, a batch can mix subsets and gradients are stabler. The 9B student is based on Qwen3.5-9B; LoRA alone underfit, so the last 8 text layers are fully fine-tuned and the rest use LoRA. The 0.6B student is pruned from Qwen3.5-0.8B by dropping 2 of 3 Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers per block (594M total; 254M embedding, 100M vision; ~240M active on text) and is fully fine-tuned.

## 3. Experiments

### 3.1 Text retrieval

This checks whether the two distilled models beat same-size single-vector models on text. The domain suite has 72 public tasks (finance 18, law 20, medical 8, dialogue 5, tech 4, multilingual 17), nDCG@10, equal-weight average over six domains:

9B leads every domain except medical; 0.6B leads every domain among sub-1B models.

Q2D-Web is closer to Perplexity's online setting: ~70K agent-rewritten online search queries over 190M web pages, Recall@1000. Relevance merges three sources: documents the agent actually cited, documents ranked high by the online retriever, and LLM-judged relevant docs. On that merge, 9B and 0.6B score 74.8% and 73.6% versus 69.3% for the strongest baseline nemotron-3-embed-8b. This benchmark comes from Perplexity traffic; other models were not tuned for it.

### 3.2 Document screenshots and images

On images it is not fully dominant. On ViDoRe-V3, vision-specialized EVIE-8B (66.4%) and EVIE-4.5B (65.9%) are higher, but they store 4,096 and 2,048 dims per token, ==while pplx-embed-v2-late stores only 128-d==. On MIRACL-Vision (Wikipedia screenshots) and PPLX-Q2I (Perplexity online image-search logs: 10K queries, 100K images), gemini-embedding-2 is higher.

### 3.3 Small-model query + large-model index

This checks whether the shared vector space is usable in deployment. Index documents with 9B; encode queries with 9B or 0.6B. 0.6B query + 9B docs beats both-ends-0.6B in all six domains, averaging 79.6% versus 78.0% (both-ends-9B is 81.3%). Query encoding cost matches pure 0.6B; document index cost is amortized over the index lifetime.

![nDCG@10 for three query/document model combinations across six domains (paper Figure 2). Dark blue = both 9B; mid blue = 0.6B query + 9B docs; light blue = both 0.6B.](figs/2610.29523/fig2_cross_model.png)

### 3.4 As the retriever for a search agent

BrowseComp+ lets GPT-OSS-120B act as an agent that repeatedly searches a fixed corpus with the tested retriever and answers complex questions, scored by another LLM. 9B accuracy is 64.0%, 4.9 points above another late-interaction model Reason-ModernColBERT and 8.7 above the best single-vector voyage-4-large; ==mean search count is also lower than every baseline==, and recall is highest.

![BrowseComp+ answer accuracy (left) and retrieval recall (right); x-axis is mean search count—upper-left is better (paper Figure 3).](figs/2610.29523/fig3_browsecomp.png)

## 4. Limitations

No storage or latency numbers are given. Multi-vector indexes store a 128-d vector per token; how much more storage and MaxSim cost that is versus single-vector at web scale is unstated. The domain-task list is private, so scores cannot be reproduced. On image retrieval, specialized vision models and gemini-embedding-2 still win on some benchmarks. The claim that distillation beats pure contrastive learning—especially for small models—has no contrastive numbers in the body.

## 5. Takeaways

For retrieval teams, the most directly usable piece is "large model indexes, small model queries": document compute is paid once, query latency is 0.6B, and quality beats a pure small model by 1.6 points. The premise is that both ends are distilled from the same teacher; independently trained models cannot be mixed this way. The 0.6B text side has only ~240M active parameters; the authors argue it can run on-device. If you are evaluating multi-vector retrieval, measure storage on your own corpus first—that is the unanswered question in the report.

papers.title: Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion for Query Reformulation in Dense Retrieval
papers.authors: Yiteng Tu, Qingyi Pan, Weihang Su, Jiaxin Mao, Yiqun Liu, Qingyao Ai
papers.summary: When rewriting a query vector with first-round retrieved documents or an LLM-written hypothetical answer (HyDE), the usual approach averages feedback vectors and interpolates with the original query. DIFF argues that ==each piece of feedback only supports correcting the query along one direction, so other directions should not be pulled back by it==: it subtracts the component parallel to the original query to get each feedback's rotation direction and magnitude, constrains only the projection of the correction onto that direction, weights by query–feedback similarity and group agreement, and solves a K×K linear system—without training any model. On 14 BEIR subsets, bge-base with HyDE rises from 0.5492 to 0.5717 mean NDCG@10; with retrieved-document feedback, vector averaging falls to 0.5045 while DIFF scores 0.5522.

deep_reading.title: Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion for Query Reformulation in Dense Retrieval
deep_reading.content:
In vector retrieval, short queries often under-specify intent. A common fix is to gather feedback text—top documents from a first-round search, or an LLM-written hypothetical answer (HyDE)—and use it to update the query vector. Most methods average the feedback vectors or linearly interpolate with the original query, treating each feedback as "what the new query should look like" and pulling the query toward it as a whole. Tsinghua's DIFF argues that this causes interference: ==each piece of feedback usually supports correcting the query along only one direction; other directions carry no information from it, yet are still pulled back==. DIFF first extracts the direction each feedback adds beyond the original query, requires the corrected query to agree with the feedback only along that direction, weights constraints by feedback quality, adds a "do not drift too far from the original" term, and has a closed-form solution that needs no training. On 14 BEIR subsets, 3 retrievers, and 4 feedback sources, DIFF's mean NDCG@10 is best or tied for best in 12 of 12 settings, but with first-round retrieved documents as feedback it barely improves over the unfeedbacked query.

## 1. Treating feedback as target points loses complementary information

Let the original query be $q$ and the correction proposed by feedback $i$ relative to $q$ be $e_i=\ell_i u_i$, with unit direction $u_i$ and magnitude $\ell_i$. Pointwise fitting minimizes $\|\delta-\ell_i u_i\|^2$. The authors split it:

$$\lVert\delta-\ell_i u_i\rVert^2=(u_i^\top\delta-\ell_i)^2+\lVert(I-u_iu_i^\top)\delta\rVert^2$$

The first term asks $\delta$'s component along $u_i$ to equal $\ell_i$—desired. The second penalizes $\delta$ on every other direction, which may be exactly what other feedback supports. Example: query "apple event"; one feedback doc is about a new phone, another about a new laptop; pointwise fitting pulls the query halfway between them and travels only halfway on each direction.

They prove that under the same weights, directional constraints yield a correction magnitude at least as large as pointwise fitting, with equality only when all feedback directions are collinear; when feedback directions are pairwise orthogonal, pointwise fitting dilutes each direction's correction by the other feedbacks' weights.

![Two fusion styles (paper Figure 1). Left: pointwise fitting pulls $\delta$ toward the middle of $e_1$ and $e_2$. Right: directional constraints; each feedback only constrains $\delta$'s projection on its own direction, so $\delta$ can satisfy both.](figs/2610.29464/fig1_point_vs_direction.png)

## 2. Method: four steps

**Step 1: new direction per feedback.** All vectors are L2-normalized on the unit sphere. For feedback $f_i$, compute similarity $s_i=q^\top f_i$, then subtract the component parallel to $q$ to get $r_i=f_i-s_iq$. Direction $u_i$ is where this feedback wants to rotate the query; length $\ell_i$ equals the sine of their angle—how much new content it adds.

**Step 2: credibility per feedback.** Credibility $\tau_i=g\cdot a_i$ has two layers. Per-item quality $a_i$: standardize the $s_i$ values under the same query by median and MAD, then pass through a sigmoid, so feedback closer to the query weighs more without depending on absolute similarity scales across models. Group credibility $g$: mean of all correction vectors $\mu$, then compare $\|\mu\|^2$ to dispersion around that mean; $g$ is high when directions agree and low when they conflict, then multiplied by mean per-item quality.

**Step 3: jointly solve for the correction.** The objective keeps only each feedback's own-direction constraint plus a penalty on correction size:

$$\delta^*=\arg\min_{\delta}\ \frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\delta\rVert^2+\frac12\sum_i\tau_i(u_i^\top\delta-\ell_i)^2$$

It has a closed form: solve a $K\times K$ linear system ($K$ feedbacks, 5 in the main experiment), cost $O(K^2D+K^3)$ for dimension $D$.

**Step 4: map back to the sphere.** The final rotation angle is the min of $\|\delta^*\|$ and "$g$ × max allowed angle", then $q'=\cos\phi\,q+\sin\phi\,\delta^*/\|\delta^*\|$. When the group is untrustworthy, $g$ is small and the query barely moves.

## 3. Experiments

Setup: 14 BEIR subsets (ArguAna, FEVER, HotpotQA, MSMARCO, NQ, SciFact, TREC-COVID, …), three retrievers bge-base-en-v1.5, e5-base-v2, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. Feedback is either the top-$K$ first-round documents (PRF) or three Qwen3.8-27B generations (HyDE hypothetical docs, Q2D query expansion, CoT reasoning). All methods share the same encoder, the same feedback, and the same index—only fusion differs. Baselines include vector averaging (VPRF), concatenate-and-reencode (Concat-P/L), orthogonal-component OR-PRF, dimension-weighted DIME and Eclipse, and AnchorQE which needs extra retrieval to estimate weights.

### 3.1 Main results

This checks whether DIFF beats other fusion methods across retrievers and feedback sources. Mean NDCG@10 over 14 subsets; parentheses are the unfeedbacked query:

Two results stand out. First, with retrieved-document feedback, simple averaging (VPRF) pulls scores below the original query—on BGE from 0.5492 to 0.5045; ==DIFF in that column merely does not lose==: 0.5522 on BGE, 0.5252 on E5, 0.5491 on Qwen, barely changing versus the original. Second, with LLM-generated feedback every method gains; DIFF reaches 0.5717 on BGE with HyDE and 0.5777 on Qwen. It is close to AnchorQE (0.5717 vs 0.5700 on BGE + HyDE) but needs no extra retrieval for weights.

### 3.2 Ablations

This checks whether directional constraints and credibility weighting are each necessary. On BGE, remove or replace one part at a time:

Switching back to pointwise fitting is among the largest drops, directly supporting the paper's core claim: constraining each feedback only along its own direction beats pulling the query toward feedback as a whole. Dropping per-item quality under HyDE falls from 0.5717 to 0.5481—generated hypothetical docs vary in quality and must be treated differently.

### 3.3 Feedback count

As $K$ grows from 1 to 20, VPRF drops quickly under retrieved-document feedback because later documents are noisier. DIFF stays stable across $K$; the authors attribute this to group credibility shrinking the correction when feedback becomes mixed.

## 4. Limitations

The main-table point: with first-round retrieved documents as feedback, DIFF barely beats the unfeedbacked query and is slightly worse on Qwen (0.5491 vs 0.5492). Its value is mainly "not being dragged down by noise" and "using generated feedback well." Experiments are only on BEIR with retrievers up to 0.6B; production-scale corpora and larger embedding models are untested. Group credibility and max rotation angle have hyperparameters whose sensitivity is not analyzed in the body.

## 5. Takeaways

If you already use HyDE or query expansion and average the encoded text with the original query, consider DIFF: it depends only on vectors, needs no training and no extra retrieval, and solves one 5×5 linear system per query. If feedback is first-round retrieval, this paper's results say gains are limited—at least confirm that averaging is not already hurting metrics.

Group credibility and max rotation angle have hyperparameters whose sensitivity is not analyzed in the body.

5. Takeaways

If you already use HyDE or query expansion and average the encoded text with the original query, consider DIFF: it depends only on vectors, needs no training and no extra retrieval, and solves one 5×5 linear system per query. If feedback is first-round retrieval, this paper's results say gains are limited—at least confirm that averaging is not already hurting metrics.

papers.title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
papers.authors: Juan Terven, Diana-Margarita C\'ordova-Esparza, Julio-Alejandro Romero-Gonz\'alez, Edgar Chavez-Urbiola, Juan Irving Vasquez, Julian Andres Ramirez-Bautista, Silvia L. Chaparro-C\'ardenas, Gendry Alfonso-Francia
papers.summary: For long-document QA, should you build a vector index then retrieve, or let the model scan the full text segment by segment each time? The authors compare 11 setups on 396 QASPER paper questions and 80 questions from 8 full textbooks, fixing chunking, a top-5 segment budget, and the same answer model. On textbooks, hybrid retrieval plus Jev reranking reaches the highest evidence coverage (94.1%), Jev full-text scan 88.7%, and OpenAI vector retrieval 81.3%: even though full-text scan sees every segment, ==later filtering drops relevant segments==. ==Higher evidence coverage does not mean better answers==; the highest answer accuracy is hybrid retrieval plus OpenAI Decisions reranking (0.892). When queries are many, a reusable vector index costs the least.

papers.title: An Explicit Feedback Contract for Iterative ML-Agent Harnesses
papers.authors: Kehui Yao, Chuanbo Hu, Jiao Chen, Ramin Giahi, Reza Yousefi Maragheh, Lalitesh Morishetti, Ziwei Hong, Yiyun Su, Jianpeng Xu, Evren Korpeoglu, Kannan Achan
papers.summary: When an ML agent edits code, runs experiments, reads validation scores, and chooses the next step, it keeps changes that happen to look better on that validation set. Walmart defines a feedback rule for this loop: only tell the agent the validation score when the lift over the current best exceeds a noise threshold from paired standard error, and specify when to stop and when the test set may be touched. On a ==control task constructed so no real lift is possible==, an agent that sees exact scores reports a final lift of 0.0157, versus 0.0033 under the rule. On Criteo CTR and MSLR ranking, validation–test gaps shrink and test scores are slightly higher; with exact scores 2 of 3 tasks use all 30 submissions, while the rule stops at 4–12.

papers.title: How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage
papers.summary: This NVIDIA tutorial shows how to use KvikIO in Python to read files straight into GPU memory without a CPU bounce buffer (GPUDirect Storage). ==Each read takes two routing decisions==: KvikIO first chooses cuFile or its own POSIX-compatible path, and reads below a threshold (16 KiB in the tutorial) go POSIX; cuFile then chooses the nvidia-fs accelerated path or a CPU-mediated compatibility path. The two choices are controlled by KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE, KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD, and parallel-split settings in cufile.json. To confirm the accelerated path ran, set CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and check whether gds_stats counts land in the nvfs or posix column.

papers.title: The science behind TorchNeuron, Amazon’s new PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips
papers.summary: TorchNeuron is Amazon's open-source PyTorch backend for running models on Trainium. Optional adaptive eager mode batches operators into small graphs that a background compiler compiles, caches, and queues, picking a split strategy by graph size so ==compilation overlaps with execution of already-compiled work== and approaches full-graph compile speed. Artifacts use memory and disk caches, and accelerators on one server share a compile service; on a large cross-accelerator model, time to the first training step falls by about one third. For testing, an AI agent picks 841 representative models by structural features from hundreds of thousands on Hugging Face for tuning and regression.

papers.title: Running Frontier-Class AI Models Across 8 NVIDIA DGX Spark Nodes
papers.summary: NVIDIA announces that DGX Spark officially supports an 8-node cluster, each with 128 GB unified memory (1 TB total), enough to run full GLM 5.3 locally (753B, ~470 GB in NVFP4): about 1,600 token/s single-concurrency prefill and 31 token/s decode. Under switch networking, the RoCEnante collective backend ==cuts all-reduce latency in tensor-parallel decode==, raising the 8-node decode speedup from 3.05× to 4.43×. Pretraining nanochat from scratch on 8 nodes speeds up 7.79× with 97.4% scaling efficiency.

papers.title: PACE: Periodic and Channel-Aligned Encoding of Four-Bit Recurrent States
papers.authors: Patrick Haller, Filipe Laitenberger, Alan Akbik
papers.summary: Linear-attention models keep a fixed-size recurrent state per decoding sequence; the cheaper the state, the more sequences one GPU can serve. Prior work quantizes the state every token and quality drops sharply at 4 bits. PACE quantizes every few tokens and buffers the in-between tokens; it also finds that ==large values in gated delta state cluster by column, so each column shares one quantization scale==; a few heads that accumulate error keep 8 bits. On four hybrid models from 4B to 35B, a 4/8-bit mix matches 8-bit DAMP on the three larger models at about two-thirds the memory; pure 4-bit beats Q-Mamba at equal memory.

papers.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
papers.authors: Qiuyang Mang, Wenhao Chai, Runyuan He, Dongruixuan Li, Zihan Zheng
papers.summary: FrontierCS 2 tests whether AI agents can do computer-science research: take a paper and the authors' public code, remove the paper's core contribution, and require the agent to reimplement it in that repo and beat the removed original. Forty-eight tasks span 13 areas including ML systems, HPC, databases, security, and robotics; agents may submit patches anytime for a dev-set score and are judged on a held-out test set against the original. Among 12 agents, Claude Opus 5.5 is best with 58% of runs passing; 16 tasks see no passing run. ==Runs whose aggregate score beats the original still usually miss some metric or workload==.

papers.title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory
papers.summary: Memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to store before a question arrives; coding agents keep the raw dialogue and let the model search with tools. On one LoCoMo dialogue (419 turns, 152 questions) the authors run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code) with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna, and Claude Opus 5.5, logging cost each time. Mem0 beats full context only under GPT-4o-mini, and ==building the memory alone costs more than one full-context QA==; with Claude Opus 5.5, Pi answers 99% correctly at under half the full-context cost. Each combo is run once; the authors note the study is small.
